content: Red birthmarks are vascular skin markings that are either present at birth or develop shortly thereafter. These birthmarks are caused by blood vessels close to the skin's surface. Symptoms of Red Birthmarks: Red birthmarks appear as skin markings resembling blood vessels or as red skin lesions. Different types of red birthmarks have distinct appearances and typical locations: Cavernous hemangiomas: These present as red-blue, spongy masses of tissue filled with blood. Port-wine stains: These are most commonly found on the face and can range in size from very small to covering over half of the body surface. Salmon patches: These are small, pink, flat spots caused by visible capillaries under the skin. They are commonly located on the forehead, eyelids, upper lip, between the eyebrows, and the back of the neck. They may become more noticeable when the infant cries or during temperature changes. Strawberry hemangiomas: These can appear anywhere on the body but are most common on the neck and face. They consist of small, closely packed blood vessels. Causes of Red Birthmarks: Red birthmarks, also known as vascular birthmarks, are composed of blood vessels near the skin's surface. Their exact cause is unknown, but the red coloration results from the development of blood vessels in the affected area. Types of vascular birthmarks include: Strawberry hemangiomas: These may develop several weeks after birth and are also referred to as capillary hemangiomas or nevus vascularis. Cavernous hemangiomas: These are similar to strawberry hemangiomas but are located deeper in the skin. Salmon patches: Also known as stork bites, these are extremely common and occur in 30-50% of newborns. Port-wine stains: These are flat hemangiomas made of dilated blood capillaries. When located on the face, they may be associated with Sturge-Weber syndrome. Diagnosis: A healthcare provider should examine all birthmarks. Diagnosis is primarily based on the appearance of the skin lesion. Additional tests to confirm deeper birthmarks may include: Biopsy CT scan MRI of the affected area When to Seek Medical Care: All birthmarks should be evaluated by a healthcare provider to determine the need for treatment, assess potential complications, and predict the likely outcome. Treatment Options: Many strawberry hemangiomas, cavernous hemangiomas, and salmon patches are temporary and do not require treatment. Port-wine stains and other permanent birthmarks may not need treatment unless they are disfiguring, psychologically distressing, painful, or change in appearance. Concealing cosmetics, such as Covermark, can be used to hide permanent birthmarks. Cortisone, either oral or injected, may reduce the size of a rapidly growing hemangioma that obstructs vision or vital organs. Permanent birthmarks are usually not treated unless they cause symptoms or until the child reaches school age. However, port-wine stains on the face should be treated at a young age with a yellow pulsed-dye laser to prevent psychological and social issues. Treatment options include: Cryotherapy (freezing) Laser surgery Surgical removal Prognosis: Birthmarks rarely cause problems beyond cosmetic concerns. Many birthmarks fade or disappear by the time a child reaches school age, but some are permanent. Strawberry hemangiomas: These typically grow quickly, stabilize, and then regress. About 95% disappear by the time the child is 9 years old, though slight discoloration or puckering of the skin may remain. Cavernous hemangiomas: Some disappear on their own, usually as the child approaches school age. Port-wine stains: These are often permanent. Salmon patches: These often fade as the infant grows. Patches on the back of the neck may not fade but are usually hidden by hair growth. Possible Complications: Emotional distress due to appearance Discomfort or occasional bleeding from vascular birthmarks Scarring or complications following surgical removal Prevention: There is no known way to prevent the development of birthmarks.
